← Universe at Scale

Credits & sources

Everything on these maps sits where published measurements put it. This page lists where those measurements come from, who took the pictures, and what is drawn to illustrate rather than measured. On the galaxy map, each object's card also names the measurement behind its distance.

The Solar System

  • Planets: NASA JPL Keplerian orbital elements (E. M. Standish), valid 1800–2050; Jupiter, Saturn and Uranus from the VSOP87 planetary theory (Bretagnon & Francou 1988).
  • Dwarf planets: JPL Small-Body Database; Ceres and Pluto from JPL Horizons orbits every five years, blended.
  • Our Moon: Jean Meeus, Astronomical Algorithms, ch. 47 (ELP-2000/82), with ΔT from Espenak & Meeus; tables from the open-source astronomia library.
  • Other moons: JPL mean orbital elements (ssd.jpl.nasa.gov), each moon's place and pace fitted to JPL Horizons over 1800–2050; Triton and Mimas from Horizons directly. Moon counts: Minor Planet Center, mid-2026.
  • Spacecraft: Voyager 1, Voyager 2 and New Horizons trajectories from JPL Horizons.
  • Spin and tilt: IAU rotation models (Archinal et al. 2018); Earth's precession, IAU 2006.
  • Stars in the sky: the same AT-HYG catalogue as the galaxy map (below).
  • Eclipses: found from the same Sun and Moon positions as the rest of the map (Meeus' lunar theory, JPL orbits), 1800–2050; checked against NASA's eclipse catalogue.
  • Galactic motion: the Sun's speed and direction around the Galaxy, Reid et al. 2019.

The Milky Way

  • Stars: 9,407 stars placed by their measured parallax — AT-HYG v3.2 by David Nash (CC BY-SA 4.0), built on Gaia DR3 and Hipparcos. Star colours from their B−V colour (Ballesteros 2012).
  • The Sun's place: 8.275 kpc from the centre (GRAVITY Collaboration 2021), 20.8 pc above the midplane (Bennett & Bovy 2019).
  • Spiral arms: maser parallaxes, Reid et al. 2019 — solid where measured, dashed where extrapolated.
  • The galactic centre: the star S2 (GRAVITY Collaboration 2020) and the S-stars (Gillessen et al. 2017); the young-star disc (Yelda et al. 2014); the minispiral (Zhao et al. 2009); the circumnuclear disc (Jackson 1993; Christopher et al. 2005; Lau et al. 2013); the view of Sgr A* (Event Horizon Telescope 2022). The black hole is ray-traced from general relativity.
  • The Sun's orbit: traced from Reid et al. 2019 through a Galaxy model fitted to the local disc density (McKee et al. 2015; Bovy & Rix 2013).
  • Nebulae, clusters and stars: each card names its distance source — mostly Gaia parallaxes (e.g. Kuhn et al. 2019, 2020; Göppl & Preibisch 2022; Baumgardt & Vasiliev 2021) and radio parallaxes (e.g. Dodson et al. 2003; Miller-Jones et al. 2021).
  • Other star systems: TRAPPIST-1 (Agol et al. 2021); Alpha Centauri (Akeson et al. 2021; Kervella et al. 2017; Faria et al. 2022; candidate planet, Beichman et al. 2025); habitable zones (Kopparapu et al. 2014).
  • Pulsars and magnetars: Kramer et al. 2021; Reardon et al. 2024; NICER; Ng & Romani 2004; the McGill Magnetar Catalog (Olausen & Kaspi 2014), with each magnetar's distance source on its card.

Beyond the Milky Way

  • Nearby galaxies: distances from eclipsing binaries, Cepheids, the tip of the red giant branch and supernovae (e.g. Pietrzyński et al. 2019; Graczyk et al. 2020; Li et al. 2021; Anand et al. 2018, 2021; Jang et al. 2020; McQuinn et al. 2017; Radburn-Smith et al. 2011; Schweizer et al. 2008); the Sagittarius Dwarf (Hamanowicz et al. 2016; Vasiliev & Belokurov 2020).
  • Their futures: Andromeda (Sawala et al. 2025); the Large Magellanic Cloud (Cautun et al. 2019).
  • Cosmic voids: Cosmicflows-3 (Tully et al. 2019); Kirshner et al. 1981; Kopylov & Kopylova 2002; Szapudi et al. 2015; Keenan, Barger & Cowie 2013 (disputed).
  • Laniakea: Tully et al. 2014; Cosmicflows-4 (Valade et al. 2024).
  • Quasars: 3C 273 (GRAVITY Collaboration 2018); TON 618 (Ge et al. 2019); J0529-4351 (Wolf et al. 2024); the Einstein Cross (Sluse et al. 2011); accretion discs after Shakura & Sunyaev 1973.
  • The farthest things seen: MoM-z14 (Naidu et al. 2025); JADES-GS-z14-0 (Carniani et al. 2024; Schouws et al. 2025); GN-z11 (Bunker et al. 2023; Maiolino et al. 2024); Earendel (Welch et al. 2022).
  • Far-away clusters: the Bullet Cluster (Clowe et al. 2006); El Gordo (Menanteau et al. 2012); Pandora's Cluster (UNCOVER, Bezanson et al. 2024); SMACS 0723 (Webb Early Release Observations, 2022).
  • The largest structures: the Sloan Great Wall (Gott et al. 2005; Sheth & Diaferio 2011); the Giant Arc (Lopez, Clowes & Williger 2022) and the Big Ring (Lopez, Clowes & Williger 2024), both debated.
  • The cosmic microwave background: the Planck 2018 map (ESA and the Planck Collaboration, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons); distance to where its light left, from the Planck 2018 cosmology.
  • Distances across the universe: Planck 2018 cosmology, giving both comoving distance and light-travel time.

Pictures

  • Moon: NASA’s Scientific Visualization Studio CGI Moon Kit (public domain): the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter’s Wide Angle Camera colour mosaic, with the relief from its laser altimeter (LOLA) elevation model.
  • Earth: Solar System Scope (CC BY 4.0), based on NASA Blue Marble and Black Marble imagery.
  • Planet surfaces (photographs): Mercury — NASA/JHU APL MESSENGER MDIS global mosaic (Commons; monochrome, with Mercury's faint brownish grey added); Mars — NASA/JPL/USGS Viking Orbiter colour mosaic MDIM 2.1 (Commons); Jupiter — NASA/JPL/Space Science Institute, Cassini, December 2000 (PIA07782, Commons), with Juno's views of the poles laid over it: the north from NASA/JPL-Caltech/SwRI/MSSS, Gerald Eichstädt and John Rogers (PIA24237, CC BY; labels painted out), the south from NASA/JPL-Caltech/SwRI/MSSS, Betsy Asher Hall and Gervasio Robles (PIA21641); both released colour-enhanced and toned toward natural colour here; Saturn, Uranus and Neptune — Solar System Scope (CC BY 4.0), built from Cassini and Voyager 2 imagery (Commons); Pluto — NASA/JHU APL/SwRI New Horizons global colour mosaic (Commons; the side New Horizons saw from afar is blurrier).
  • The Sun: drawn for this site in true colour — white, as it looks from space — with limb darkening (the edge dimmer and warmer), granulation (sped up so you can watch it boil), sunspots and faculae, and rotation on its real axis every 25.4 days, all following observations. The magnetic network's pattern, after NASA SDO's pictures, is made stronger than the eye would see it so the texture shows; the sunspots are illustrative, not today's.
  • Planet relief (the slopes along the day–night line): Mercury — USGS Astrogeology / NASA / JHU APL / ASU, MESSENGER global DEM 665 m, v2 2016 (Commons); Mars — NASA Goddard Space Flight Center, MOLA (Mars Global Surveyor) topography map (Commons), its colour scale read back into heights, so levels are approximate. Slopes are exaggerated a few times so the relief shows at planetary scale. Pluto has no global elevation map yet, so it is shown without relief.
  • Venus' surface: NASA/JPL Magellan radar map, via Wikimedia Commons.
  • Titan's surface: NASA/JPL-Caltech/University of Nantes/University of Arizona, Cassini (PIA22770), via Wikimedia Commons.
  • Moon surfaces (photographs): Io — USGS Astrogeology, Galileo/Voyager merged mosaic (Commons); Europa — colour map from Galileo and Voyager images by Seek9750 (CC0, Commons); Ganymede and Callisto — Askaniy Anpilogov, from USGS, Björn Jónsson, John van Vliet and Juno (NASA/JPL-Caltech/SwRI/MSSS/Brian Swift) data (CC BY-SA 3.0, Ganymede, Callisto); Mimas, Enceladus, Tethys, Dione, Rhea and Iapetus — NASA/JPL-Caltech/Space Science Institute/Lunar and Planetary Institute, Cassini global colour maps (PIA18434–39), released in enhanced colour and toned back toward natural here; Triton — NASA/JPL/USGS, Voyager 2, map by Paul Schenk (LPI) (Commons); Charon — NASA/JHU APL/SwRI, New Horizons (Commons); Titania, Umbriel and Oberon — Caltech/JPL/USGS, Voyager 2; Phobos and Deimos — Askaniy Anpilogov, from Viking and Mars Express data (CC BY-SA 3.0). Where a spacecraft never saw part of a moon in daylight (Triton's and Uranus' moons' north, Charon's south) it is filled plainly with the moon's average colour. Each moon's overall brightness is set from its measured albedo.
  • Other planets and moons: painted for this site from their real colours and banding, not photographs.

Photographs of nebulae, clusters and galaxies are shown from Wikimedia Commons; each object's card on the map also credits its picture.

What is illustrative

These parts are drawn to show what something is like, not where it is measured to be:

  • Where most small moons sit along their orbits (each card says whether a moon's position is real).
  • The dots of the Oort cloud — its shape and size are predicted, not seen.
  • The Milky Way's glow and the far side of its spiral arms — a model built on the measured arms. Its star clouds, dust lanes and pink nebulae are painted to look like a real barred spiral, not mapped one by one.
  • Magnetic field lines, the clumps of gas near Sgr A*, the inner workings of quasars, and the spin axes of most pulsars and magnetars.
  • The round outlines of Laniakea and the voids — their real boundaries are irregular.
  • The shapes of the Sloan Great Wall, the Giant Arc and the Big Ring are simplified lines along their measured spines; the Big Ring's position is approximate.
  • In the sky view, the ground, trees, grass, wind, clouds and seasons are drawn to look natural but are not any real place or weather; the stars, Sun, Moon, planets and Milky Way are where they really were.
  • The cosmic microwave background is drawn as a see-through shell so what's inside stays visible; the pattern on it is Planck's real map.
  • In Galactic motion, the Sun's speed is slowed down so the corkscrews show; the slider says by how much, and "True speed" shows it as it is.
  • The older half of the Sun's orbit: the bar and spiral arms tug on it, so it is uncertain by a few thousand light-years.
